nameStory: The "red" in red hickory comes from the reddish-brown color of its inner bark and wood when freshly cut. It's also called sweet pignut hickory because its nuts are sweeter and more palatable than those of its close relative, the regular pignut hickory. The name reflects both its appearance and its more appetizing nuts!
description: Red hickory is a medium-sized deciduous tree that typically grows 50-80 feet tall with a straight trunk and oval-shaped crown. It's one of New England's rarer hickory species, found scattered in dry upland forests. Like other hickories, it has compound leaves with 5-7 leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand, and produces hard-shelled nuts enclosed in thick husks that split open when ripe. The tree has smooth gray bark when young that develops shallow furrows with age.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 5-7 leaflets (usually 5) arranged palmately like fingers on a hand. Leaflets are lance-shaped, 3-6 inches long, with finely serrated edges and a smooth, slightly glossy surface that feels firm to the touch.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth light gray bark on young trees that develops shallow, interlacing ridges as it matures - never the shaggy, peeling plates of shagbark hickory. When scratched or cut, the inner bark reveals a distinctive reddish-brown color.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round to egg-shaped nuts about 1 inch long, enclosed in thin husks that split halfway to the base when ripe. The nuts are sweet and edible, with a thinner shell than most other hickory nuts, making them easier to crack.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Winter buds are small (less than 1/2 inch), egg-shaped, and covered with overlapping yellowish-brown to reddish-brown scales. Terminal buds are larger than side buds and help distinguish it from other hickories.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a straight trunk with an oval crown, typically found on dry ridges and slopes. The branching pattern creates a relatively open canopy compared to other forest trees, allowing dappled sunlight to reach the forest floor.

habitat: Red hickory thrives in dry, well-drained sandy soils on upland ridges and sloped woodlands throughout New England, though it's quite uncommon here. Look for it in mixed hardwood forests alongside oaks, maples, and other hickories, typically on south-facing slopes and ridge tops where the soil drains quickly. It prefers these drier sites over the moister valleys where other hickories might be found.

seasonality.spring: Small yellowish-green flowers appear in late spring as leaves emerge. Male flowers hang in drooping catkins while female flowers are tiny and inconspicuous at branch tips.
seasonality.summer: Full compound leaves create filtered shade, and developing nuts begin forming in small green husks. This is when the glossy green leaflets are most distinctive for identification.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn golden-yellow before dropping, and nuts ripen with husks splitting partway open to reveal the sweet hickory nuts inside. Fall is the best time to find and taste the nuts.
seasonality.winter: Bare trees show the distinctive smooth-to-furrowed bark pattern and small, scaly buds. The oval crown shape and branching pattern are most visible without leaves.

funFact: Red hickory nuts are considered the tastiest of all the hickory nuts - early settlers and Native Americans specifically sought them out because they're sweet enough to eat raw and have thinner shells that don't require a hammer to crack open like other hickory nuts!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with pignut hickory, its close relative, but red hickory has consistently 5 leaflets (pignut usually has 7), sweeter nuts, and reddish inner bark when scratched. Memory trick: "Red hickory, five fingers" - count the leaflets and scratch the bark to check for red coloring underneath.
contextualKnowledge: This species has a confusing taxonomic history - some botanists still consider it just a variety of pignut hickory rather than its own species. You might see it listed as Carya glabra var. odorata in older field guides, which explains why identification between these two species can be tricky even for experts.
compareHints: Red hickory differs from shagbark hickory by having smooth bark instead of distinctive shaggy plates, and from pignut hickory by typically having 5 leaflets instead of 7, plus sweeter nuts and reddish inner bark. Unlike bitternut hickory, its buds are brown rather than bright yellow, and unlike mockernut, its leaflets are smooth rather than fuzzy underneath.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's hickories, shagbark is the only one with bark that peels in long, dramatic strips - other hickories have tight, furrowed bark.
Among New England hickories, bitternut is the easiest to identify thanks to its unique yellow buds.
Pignut hickory has much smoother bark than the dramatically peeling shagbark hickory, and smaller, less noticeable buds than the large, fuzzy-budded mockernut hickory.

Among New England hickories, mockernut is the only one with consistently fuzzy leaf undersides - shagbark hickory has peeling bark plates, bitternut has bright yellow buds, and pignut has smooth leaves and smaller nuts.
Among New England hickories, shellbark stands out for its larger nuts and more dramatic bark peeling compared to shagbark hickory.
